claims.text: Controlled thermal oxidation of Q235 steel at 250°C produces an oxide film with protective thickness, composition, and integrity.
The oxide film produced at 250°C suppresses chloride-related corrosion at room temperature and 60°C.
Thermal oxidation at 400°C produces an overly thick or non-uniform oxide film.
The oxide film produced at 400°C fails to protect Q235 steel and can facilitate localized corrosion.
Q235 steel in the initial state has a native oxide film.
Heating Q235 steel in dry air at 250°C for 1–2 hours will form the proposed optimal oxide scale.
Heating Q235 steel in dry air at 400°C for 1–2 hours will form a thicker and potentially less adherent oxide scale.
Oxide-film thickness, composition, and integrity govern the corrosion response of the treated steel.
An intact, optimally formed oxide film acts as a physical barrier to aggressive-ion penetration.
Inhibiting aggressive-ion penetration slows the onset of corrosion.
Excessively thick, non-uniform, or cracked oxide films can create stress concentrations or local defects that promote localized-corrosion initiation.
Relative to untreated Q235 steel, samples oxidized at 250°C will have lower corrosion rates, more uniform corrosion morphology, and delayed degradation onset.
Relative to untreated Q235 steel, samples oxidized at 400°C may exhibit accelerated localized corrosion because of compromised film integrity.
The predicted ranking of corrosion behavior will occur in 3.5% NaCl at both room temperature and 60°C.
Elevated temperature may amplify the corrosion differences among the untreated, 250°C-treated, and 400°C-treated samples.
The proposed study compares untreated, 250°C-treated, and 400°C-treated Q235 samples under otherwise identical 3.5% NaCl exposures at room temperature and 60°C.
